parts.text: Which claim correctly explains leap-day adjustments?

options.text: Solar calendars add a leap day about every four years because the extra quarter-days add up to about one full day.
Leap days are arbitrary extras that are unrelated to Earth's revolution around the Sun.
Solar calendars ignore seasons and only track the Moon's phases.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

stem: Rohan reads that Earth takes nearly 365.25 days to revolve around the Sun, and that solar calendars keep seasons aligned.

part_answers.answer: The extra quarter-day each year accumulates, so a leap day keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons.

teacher.key_rationale: Earth's revolution takes nearly 365.25 days, so solar calendars add a leap day about every four years to stay synchronised with seasons. Leap days are not arbitrary, and solar calendars are built around the Sun-year and seasons, not only Moon phases.
